sections.html: Since 1851 Baltimore has stood apart from any county, so city offices do work that a county government does elsewhere, from collecting taxes to keeping land records. It counted 585,708 residents in 2020, well under its 1950 peak of 949,708. Rowhouses are the dominant house type, many with brick or formstone fronts, and the city is split into nine regions that match police districts. Buyers shop by neighborhood: Federal Hill, Fells Point, Canton and Locust Point in the south, Roland Park, Hampden, Charles Village and Mount Washington in the north.

sections.h2: How Baltimore real property tax is billed
sections.html:
Bills go out every July 1. The city rate is $2.248 per $100 of assessed value, and the state rate of $0.112 per $100 appears on the same bill.

  • Payment is due when the bill arrives. Pay by July 31 and you take a one-half percent discount.
  • Interest and penalties start after October 1, at 1 percent interest plus a 1 percent penalty for every month late.
  • If you live in the house, you may split the bill in two equal payments. The second is due before January 1 and carries a small fee.
  • Filing an appeal does not pause the due date. A win means a refund with interest.

Homestead Tax Credit rules hold yearly growth in taxable value to 4% for homes their owners live in. Assessments come from the state. The January 1, 2026 reassessment lifted residential values in the city 13.4% over 2023, spread across three years.

The city's tax sale takes place each May. A rental or other non-owner-occupied property can be pulled in at $250 owed, and a home with its owner in residence at $750.

WhenWhat happens
Early FebruaryFinal bill and legal notice mailed
MarchList of eligible properties published in two newspapers
First week of AprilSecond notice, covering amounts through April 30
April 30Last day to pay to avoid the sale
Third week of MayAnnual tax sale, normally
Six months after saleBuyer may sue to foreclose redemption on non-owner-occupied homes
Nine months after saleSame right for owner-occupied homes

State law sets the bidder's fees and costs, and the city cannot waive them. A Tax Sale Deferral Program shields a property for a year but leaves the debt in place.

Behind on the bill? There are two clean ways out. One is paying in full by April 30, which removes the house from the sale list. The other is selling to a buyer who clears the lien at settlement, with the balance deducted from your proceeds so the title passes free.

The second route works best when you start well before the sale date. The notices in February, March and April are your warning signs. Once the May sale happens, the clock on the buyer's right to foreclose starts, and your choices narrow fast. No lender means no appraisal or underwriting, a real help against a deadline. The lien must still be paid before the deed is recorded.

As of January 28, 2022, Baltimore had 15,032 vacant houses, about 13,560 of them privately owned. The number came out when the mayor ordered a 30-day review of how city agencies handle vacants, after a fire and collapse at a vacant house killed three firefighters.

The city housing department files receivership cases against neglected vacants and was on track to file nearly 500 in that fiscal year. If you own a vacant or inherited house, selling before a case is filed keeps the property out of that process. Open code notices and liens still have to be settled at closing, so pull them before you list.

Expect a 1.5% city transfer tax on the consideration plus a 0.5% state transfer tax, 2% in all. Recordation tax is $5 for every $500.

Transfers are processed in person at the Abel Wolman Municipal Building, Room 1B, 200 N. Holliday Street. Document processing is open to the public on Mondays and Wednesdays only. Each turn takes up to three documents, and each deed can cover up to three properties.

sections.h2: What to bring to record the deed
sections.html:
• Lien certificate, signed and notarized original deed, intake sheet, settlement sheet copy and the sales contract.
  • Proof that every open lien is paid. Clear them before you sign in.
  • Individual checks to the Director of Finance covering city transfer tax, recordation tax and any yield tax.

Simplifile is available if your closing agent prefers e-recording, which saves the trip downtown.

1. Order a lien certificate first, to learn every open tax, water or city charge against the house.
  2. Complete the state disclosure or disclaimer form and attach it to the contract.
  3. Decide who covers transfer and recordation tax. The contract fixes the split, and the settlement sheet shows it.
  4. At the table, the closing agent pays liens and taxes from your proceeds, gathers the notarized deed and carries it to Room 1B.
  5. The deed is recorded on a Monday or Wednesday, when the office is open to the public, and ownership transfers on record.

Sellers who skip the lien certificate tend to learn about surprises on closing day. A few days of checking at the start saves a delayed settlement.

sections.h2: What a Baltimore seller must disclose
sections.html:
A seller of a house with four or fewer units must give the buyer a state disclosure or disclaimer statement on or before the day the contract is signed (Maryland Real Property Code 10-702). The disclaimer says the property is sold as-is, except for known latent defects.

Sales by lenders after foreclosure, sheriff and tax sales, and fiduciary transfers from estates and trusts are exempt. If the buyer is not given the form on time, the buyer can rescind within five days after receiving it. Hand it over early and keep a signed copy, so there is no dispute later about when the buyer received it.

sections.h2: Can I sell a vacant Baltimore house as-is?
sections.html:
Yes. Maryland allows an as-is sale with a disclaimer statement, and cash buyers often prefer houses that need work. The sale does not erase anything attached to the property. Liens, tax debt and open code notices are paid or settled at closing, so a title search early in the process tells you what the final number will look like. Order it before you accept any offer.

Gather the tax bills, any city notices and the deed before you talk to buyers. Offers move faster when the paperwork is ready, and you avoid surprises at the settlement table.

faqs.q: What is the Baltimore City property tax rate?
faqs.a: The city rate is $2.248 per $100 of assessed value, plus a $0.112 state rate on the same bill.

faqs.q: When are Baltimore property taxes due?
faqs.a: Bills are mailed July 1 and due on receipt. Interest and penalties start after October 1, and a one-half percent discount applies if you pay by July 31.

faqs.q: What is the Baltimore transfer tax?
faqs.a: The city transfer tax is 1.5% and the state transfer tax is 0.5%, a total of 2% of the consideration. Recordation tax is $5 per $500.

faqs.q: When does the Baltimore tax sale happen?
faqs.a: It is normally held in the third week of May. April 30 is the last day to pay and avoid the sale. Non-owner-occupied homes become eligible at $250 owed and owner-occupied homes at $750.

faqs.q: Where do I record a deed in Baltimore?
faqs.a: At the Abel Wolman Municipal Building, 200 N. Holliday Street, Room 1B, on Mondays and Wednesdays, or through e-recording with Simplifile. Bring the lien certificate and the notarized original deed.
